steps.prompt: Why does the last sentence use be able to and not can?
options: Because can has no future form — you must use will be able to.
Because computers are machines and not people who are able to learn things.
Because the sentence is negative rather than positive, and negatives change.
steps.answer: Because can has no future form — you must use will be able to.
steps.why: Can exists only in the present (can) and the past (could). For every other form use be able to.

steps.title: can, could, be able to
steps.html:
Timecan / couldbe able to
nowI can read a map.I am able to read a map.
pastI couldn’t read a map at ten.I wasn’t able to read a map at ten.
future—I’ll be able to read it soon.
with might—They might be able to communicate.
experience—I’ve never been able to sing.
questionCan you swim?Will you be able to come?

Can and could are followed by the base form: can read, never can to read.

Can has only two forms. For the future, the perfect, or after another modal, use be able to: will be able to, have been able to, might be able to.

In the present, can is much more natural than am able to. Use be able to in the present only for something difficult that you managed.

For a single past success, use was / were able to: The room was dark, but I was able to find the door.

In the next lesson can changes meaning: it will be about permission, not ability.

steps.title: Four things people believe about the brain
steps.sub: Four beliefs, and what the research actually says.
steps.html:
Reading

The brain is an amazing organ. It can learn, it can remember and it can think. It is also the subject of more myths than almost anything else in science.

Myth one: we only use ten per cent of it. We use all of it. Not all at the same time — but even a small action, like moving one finger, uses a large part of it. Nobody has ever found the other ninety per cent, because there isn’t one.

Myth two: classical music makes you cleverer. In the 1990s thousands of people bought CDs because they believed they would be able to remember more. Research says the effect is not real. You might enjoy the music anyway.

Myth three: children can’t learn two languages at once. They can, and many do. Children in bilingual homes are able to speak both languages equally well, and some research says two languages actually improve the brain.

Myth four: the brain can repair itself. Sometimes it can; sometimes it isn’t able to. It depends on how serious the damage is. This one is neither a myth nor a fact.

What about the future? Scientists believe computers will be able to scan our brains and put our thoughts into words. They won’t be able to understand those thoughts. But people with speech problems might be able to communicate just by thinking — and that alone would change many lives.

steps.title: Choose the best answer.
steps.prompt: What is the writer’s main point?
options: Most popular beliefs about the brain are myths, but one is neither true nor false.
The brain is a very much simpler organ than most ordinary people seem to think.
Scientists still know almost nothing at all about how the human brain works.
steps.answer: Most popular beliefs about the brain are myths, but one is neither true nor false.
steps.why: Three myths are answered, and the fourth — self-repair — is “neither a myth nor a fact”.
